## Appendix A Tools from Number Theory

The goal of this section is to prove Proposition 3.20. This section begins with Theorem A.30, from which the remaining proof of Proposition 3.20 will be self-contained.

### A.1 Further Group Theory and Number Theory Preliminaries

We begin with the necessary preliminaries (beyond those given in Section 3.1). We use $H_{2}(x)=x\log(1/x)+(1-x)\log(1/(1-x))$ to denote the binary entropy function with natural logarithms. Let $G$ be a group. A subgroup $H\triangleleft G$ is normal if $gHg^{-1}=H$ for all $g\in G$ , i.e. it is invariant under conjugation. The order of a group is its size $|G|$ . A normal subgroup $H\triangleleft G$ has index $[G:H]=|G/H|$ .

#### Definition A.1 (Normal Extension (Chapter 13 of [DF04])).

The extension field $K/F$ is called a splitting field for the polynomial $f(x)$ if $f(x)$ factors completely into linear factors (or splits completely) in $K[x]$ (i.e. splits into degree- $1$ polynomials with coefficients in $K$ ) and $f(x)$ does not factor completely into linear factors over any proper subfield of $K$ containing $F$ . An extension $K/F$ is normal if $K$ is the splitting field for some collection of polynomials. The normal closure of an extension $K/F$ is the smallest normal extension $K/F\subseteq N/F$ .

#### Definition A.2 (Separable (Chapter 13 of [DF04])).

A polynomial over $F$ is called separable if it has no multiple roots (i.e., all its roots are distinct). The field $K$ is said to be separable (or separably algebraic) over $F$ if every element of $K$ is the root of a separable polynomial over $F$ (equivalently, the minimal polynomial over $F$ of every element of $K$ is separable).

#### Definition A.3 (Galois Extension ([DF04, Chapter 14])).

A finite extension $K/F$ is Galois if $|\operatorname{Aut}(K/F)|=[K:F]$ . In this case, the Galois group of $K/F$ is $\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)=\operatorname{Aut}(K/F)$ .

We note that Galois extensions are normal and separable. Furthermore, since any extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ is separable, such an extension is Galois iff it is normal.

#### Definition A.4 (Fixed Field [DF04]).

If $H$ is a subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}(K/F)$ , the subfield of $K$ fixed by all the elements of $H$ is called the fixed field of $H$ , denoted $K^{H}$ .

Next, we define $p$ -groups and pro- $p$ groups.

#### Definition A.5.

A finite group $G$ is a $p$ -group if every element has order that is a power of $p$ .

#### Definition A.6 (Inverse Limits [Wil20]).

A partially ordered set $(J,\preceq)$ is an inverse system if for any $i,j\in J$ there is some $k\in J$ such that $k\preceq i$ and $k\preceq j$ .

An inverse system of groups $(J,\preceq)$ consists of: (1) group $G_{j}$ for each $j\in J$ and, whenever $i\preceq j$ , we have some homomorphism $\phi_{ij}:G_{i}\rightarrow G_{j}$ such that $\phi_{ii}=\mathrm{id}_{G_{i}}$ and $\phi_{ik}=\phi_{jk}\circ\phi_{ij}$ when $i\preceq j\preceq k$ .

The inverse limit of an inverse system of groups (more informally, the inverse limit of the groups $G_{j}$ ) is the group, denoted $\underset{\leftarrow}{\lim}G_{j}$ , of sequences $(g_{j})_{j\in J}$ such that $g_{j}\in G_{j}$ for all $j$ and $\phi_{ij}(g_{i})=g_{j}$ for all $i\preceq j$ .

#### Definition A.7 (Pro- $p$ Groups [Wil20]).

Let $p$ be a prime. A pro- $p$ group is an inverse limit of an inverse system of finite $p$ -groups.

#### Definition A.8 (Maximal unramified pro-p extension (Definition A.3 of [Ope26])).

For a number field $F$ , $F^{\mathrm{ur},p}$ denotes the compositum of all finite everywhere-unramified Galois extensions of $F$ whose Galois groups are finite $p$ -groups. Its Galois group $\operatorname{Gal}(F^{\mathrm{ur},p}/F)$ is a pro- $p$ group, and its finite quotients correspond to finite everywhere-unramified Galois $p$ -group extensions of $F$ .

Pro- $p$ groups are equipped with the following topology.

#### Definition A.9 ([Wil20]).

Let $(G_{j})_{j\in J}$ be an inverse system of finite groups. Endow each $G_{j}$ with the discrete topology (every subset is open and closed), and give $\prod G_{j}$ the product topology (open sets are the full group $G_{j}$ in all but finitely many coordinates). The topology on $\underset{\leftarrow}{\lim}\,G_{j}\subseteq\prod G_{j}$ is the subspace topology.

#### Definition A.10 (Frattini Subgroup (Definition 4.1.1 of [Wil20])).

The Frattini subgroup of group $G$ , denoted $\Phi(G)$ , is the intersection of all maximal proper subgroups of $G$ .

We define generator rank and relation rank of pro- $p$ groups.

#### Definition A.11 (Generator rank [Wil20]).

Let $G$ be a topological group and let $S$ be a subset of $G$ . We say $S$ is a (topological) generating set for $G$ if the subgroup $\langle S\rangle$ generated by $S$ is a dense subgroup of $G$ .66 6 A subset is dense if it intersects every non-empty open set. Equivalently, its closure is the whole set. The group $G$ is (topologically) finitely generated if it has a finite topological generating set. The generator rank of $G$ , denoted $d(G)$ , is the minimum size of a (topological) generating set.

For a topologically finitely generated pro- $p$ group $G$ , we have $H_{1}(G,\mathbb{F}_{p}):=G/\Phi(G)\cong\mathbb{F}_{p}^{d(G)}$ (see e.g. Proposition 4.1.13 of [Wil20], and Proposition A.26).

#### Definition A.12 (Relation rank (Section 5.4.2 of [Wil20])).

Let $G$ be a topologically finitely generated pro- $p$ group, and let $d(G)$ denote its minimal number of topological generators. A finite pro- $p$ presentation of $G$ is an isomorphism

$$ G\cong F/\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle\text{,} $$

where $F$ is a finitely generated free pro- $p$ group and $\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle$ denotes the closed normal subgroup of $F$ topologically normally generated by $R$ . The relation rank of $G$ , denoted $r(G)$ , is the minimum cardinality of such a set $R$ , taken over pro- $p$ presentations of $G$ in which $F$ is freely generated by $d(G)$ elements.

For a topologically finitely generated pro- $p$ group $G$ , one has

$$ r(G)=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}H^{2}(G,\mathbb{F}_{p})\text{,} $$

where $H^{2}$ denotes the second cohomology group (see e.g. Definition 5.1.16 and Theorem 5.4.28 of [Wil20]). In particular, $r(G)$ is intrinsic to $G$ and does not depend on the choice of a minimal topological generating set.

#### Definition A.13 (Trace (see e.g. Corollary 2.20 of [Mil20])).

Let $L/K$ be a separable extension so that there are $n=[L:K]$ distinct embeddings of $L$ fixing $K$ , denoted $\{\sigma_{i}\}$ . Then, define for $x\in L$ , $\Tr_{L/K}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}(x)$ .

#### Definition A.14 (Relative Discriminant ([Mil20])).

Let $L/K$ be a separable extension of degree $n=[L:K]$ and $x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in L$ . Then their discriminant is

$$ \disc(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=\det(\Tr_{L/K}(x_{i}x_{j}))\text{.} $$

The relative discriminant $\mathfrak{d}_{L/K}$ is the ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ generated by $\disc(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})$ for all $x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in\mathcal{O}_{L}$ .

#### Definition A.15 (Absolute Discriminant ([Mil20])).

The absolute discriminant of a number field $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is defined

$$ |\Delta_{K}|=|\disc(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})| $$

where $\{x_{i}\}$ is (any) $\mathbb{Z}$ -basis of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ .

We use the following properties of the discriminant given in [Ope26].

#### Definition A.16 (Discriminant (Definition A.6 of [Ope26])).

The root discriminant of a number field $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is $\operatorname{rd}(K)=|\Delta_{K}|^{1/[K:\mathbb{Q}]}$ . Finite unramified extensions preserve root discriminant.

For an extension $M/F$ , the relative discriminant $\mathfrak{d}_{M/F}$ is an ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{F}$ , and the tower formula is

$$ |\Delta_{M}|=|\Delta_{F}|^{[M:F]}N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{d}_{M/F}). $$

Thus $\mathfrak{d}_{M/F}=\mathcal{O}_{F}$ is equivalent to no finite ramification in $M/F$ . Here, $N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{a})=[\mathcal{O}_{F}:\mathfrak{a}]$ denotes the absolute norm of an ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ .

Next, we define the class number.

#### Definition A.17 (Fractional Ideal [Neu13]).

A fractional ideal of $K$ is a finitely generated $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ -submodule $\mathfrak{a}\neq 0$ of $K$ . The ideal group of $K$ , denoted $J_{K}$ is the group of fractional ideals of $K$ , with identity $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ and inverse $\mathfrak{a}^{-1}=\{x\in K\mid x\mathfrak{a}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{K}\}$ . The fractional principal ideals of $K$ , denoted $P_{K}$ , form a subgroup of $J_{K}$ .

#### Definition A.18 (Class Number [Neu13]).

The class group of $K$ is the group $J_{K}/P_{K}$ . The class number of $K$ , denoted $\operatorname{h}(K)$ is $\operatorname{h}(K)=|J_{K}/P_{K}|$ .

Next, we define the Frobenius representative.

#### Definition A.19 (Frobenius Representative [Mar18]).

Let $L/K$ be a Galois extension. Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ that is unramified in $L/K$ , and $\mathfrak{P}$ a prime lying above $\mathfrak{p}$ in $\mathcal{O}_{L}$ . The Frobenius automorphism of $\mathfrak{P}$ , denoted $\phi_{\mathfrak{P}}$ is the unique $\phi\in\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ such that $\phi_{\mathfrak{P}}(\alpha)\equiv\alpha^{|\mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathfrak{p}|}\pmod{\mathfrak{P}}$ for all $\alpha\in\mathcal{O}_{L}$ .

We state the necessary preliminaries for decomposition groups.

#### Definition A.20 (Decomposition Group [Mar18, Mil20]).

Let $L/K$ be an extension and $\mathfrak{p}$ a prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . For a prime $\mathfrak{P}$ above $\mathfrak{p}$ in $\mathcal{O}_{L}$ , the decomposition group $D(\mathfrak{P}\mid\mathfrak{p})$ is the set of automorphisms in $\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ satisfying $\sigma(\mathfrak{P})=\mathfrak{P}$ .

For an infinite place $v$ of $K$ and $w$ above $v$ (i.e. agreeing with $v$ on $K$ ), the decomposition group of $w$ , denoted $D_{w}$ , is the set of automorphisms in $\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ such that $\sigma(w)=w$ .

#### Definition A.21 (Chapter 7 of [Mil20]).

For any prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of number field $K$ , the $\mathfrak{p}$ -adic absolute value is given by $|x|_{\mathfrak{p}}=(1/e)^{\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(x)}$ for some constant $e>1$ . The standard choice is $e=\mathbb{N}\mathfrak{p}:=|\mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathfrak{p}|$ (Chapter 4 of [Mil20]). Let $\mathbb{Q}_{p}$ denote the completion of $\mathbb{Q}$ with the $p$ -adic absolute value.

#### Definition A.22 (Chapter 7 of [Mil20]).

Let $K$ be a field and $|\cdot|$ a non-trivial absolute value. A sequence $\{x_{i}\}$ is Cauchy if for all $\varepsilon>0$ , there exists $N$ such that $|x_{i}-x_{j}|<\varepsilon$ for all $i,j\geq N$ . A field $K$ is complete if every Cauchy sequence has a limit in $K$ .

#### Claim A.23 (Theorem 7.23 of [Mil20]).

Let $K$ be a field with an absolute value $|\cdot|$ . Then there exists a complete field $\hat{K}$ and a homomorphism $K\rightarrow\hat{K}$ preserving the absolute value that is universal in the following sense: every homomorphism $K\rightarrow L$ from $K$ into a complete field $L$ preserving the absolute value, extends uniquely to a homomorphism $\hat{K}\rightarrow L$ .

For a place $v$ of $K$ , we let $K_{v}$ denote the completion of $K$ w.r.t. $v$ . For a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ , $K_{\mathfrak{p}}$ denotes the completion of $K$ w.r.t. the $p$ -adic absolute value $|\cdot|_{\mathfrak{p}}$ .

#### Claim A.24 (Theorem 7.38, Corollary 7.42 of [Mil20]).

Then $u_{\varepsilon}c(u_{\varepsilon})=1$ . For any complex embedding $\sigma$ , the embeddings $\sigma$ and $\sigma\circ c$ are complex conjugates on the CM field, so

$$ |\sigma(u_{\varepsilon})|=\frac{|\sigma(v_{\varepsilon})|}{|\sigma(c(v_{\varepsilon}))|}=\frac{|\sigma(v_{\varepsilon})|}{|\overline{\sigma(v_{\varepsilon})}|}=1. $$

Passing from $v_{\varepsilon}$ to $v_{\varepsilon}/c(v_{\varepsilon})$ doubles these valuations, giving the displayed valuation pattern for $u_{\varepsilon}$ .

We now prove that $Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . It suffices to show that $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon})\geq 0$ for every finite prime ideal $\mathfrak{P}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . Recall that $(v_{\varepsilon})=\mathfrak{A}_{\varepsilon}\mathfrak{A}_{\eta}^{-1}$ , where $\mathfrak{A}_{\varepsilon}=\prod_{m=1}^{Tf}\mathfrak{P}_{m}^{\varepsilon_{m}}(c\mathfrak{P}_{m})^{1-\varepsilon_{m}}$ and $\mathfrak{A}_{\eta}=\prod_{m=1}^{Tf}\mathfrak{P}_{m}^{\eta_{m}}(c\mathfrak{P}_{m})^{1-\eta_{m}}$ . Thus the only prime ideals at which $v_{\varepsilon}$ can have nonzero valuation are the primes $\mathfrak{P}_{m}$ and $c\mathfrak{P}_{m}$ , all of which lie above the selected rational primes $q_{1},\dots,q_{T}$ . Moreover, for each $m$ , we have $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}_{m}}(v_{\varepsilon})=\varepsilon_{m}-\eta_{m}$ and $\operatorname{val}_{c\mathfrak{P}_{m}}(v_{\varepsilon})=(1-\varepsilon_{m})-(1-\eta_{m})=-(\varepsilon_{m}-\eta_{m})$ . Since $\varepsilon_{m},\eta_{m}\in\{0,1\}$ , the valuations all lie in $\{-1,0,1\}$ . Furthermore, $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}_{m}}(u_{\varepsilon})=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}_{m}}(v_{\varepsilon}/c(v_{\varepsilon}))=2(\varepsilon_{m}-\eta_{m})$ and similarly for $\operatorname{val}_{c\mathfrak{P}_{m}}(u_{\varepsilon})=-2(\varepsilon_{m}-\eta_{m})$ .

Now let $\mathfrak{P}$ be any finite prime of $K$ . If $\mathfrak{P}$ does not lie above any of the selected rational primes $q_{t}$ , then $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(v_{\varepsilon})=0$ and, since complex conjugation permutes the selected primes, $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(c(v_{\varepsilon}))=0$ . Hence $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(u_{\varepsilon})=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(v_{\varepsilon}/c(v_{\varepsilon}))=0$ . Since $Q^{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , we get $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon})\geq 0$ .

It remains to consider the case where $\mathfrak{P}\mid q_{t}$ for some selected rational prime $q_{t}$ . At such a prime, both $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(v_{\varepsilon})$ and $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(c(v_{\varepsilon}))$ lie in $\{-1,0,1\}$ . Therefore $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(u_{\varepsilon})=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(v_{\varepsilon})-\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(c(v_{\varepsilon}))\geq-2$ . On the other hand, $q_{t}$ splits completely in $K$ . In particular, $q_{t}$ is unramified in $K$ , so every prime $\mathfrak{P}\mid q_{t}$ has ramification index $1$ . Hence $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(q_{t})=1$ . Since $Q=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q_{t}$ , we have $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(Q^{2})=2$ . Thus $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon})=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(Q^{2})+\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(u_{\varepsilon})\geq 2-2=0$ . Therefore $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon})\geq 0$ for every finite prime $\mathfrak{P}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . Hence $Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon}$ is integral, and so $Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ .

#### Proof.

Apply Theorem A.35 with $Y=\left\lceil 4\sqrt{L}\right\rceil$ and the given $b$ . We get a CM field $K$ , a degree parameter $f\in[C_{\rm ar}b,3C_{\rm ar}b]$ , $T$ rational primes $q_{t}\in[Y,2Y]$ splitting completely in $K$ , and a family

$$ \mathcal{F}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{Tf},\qquad|\mathcal{F}|\geq e^{\gamma f}, $$

with associated elements $\{u_{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon\in\mathcal{F}}$ and $\eta$ .

We first extract many shattered valuation coordinates. Let

$$ M:=Tf,\qquad s:=(3C_{\rm ar}+2)b. $$

Since $f\geq C_{\rm ar}b$ , we have

$$ \frac{s}{M}\leq\frac{(3C_{\rm ar}+2)b}{TC_{\rm ar}b}\leq\frac{4}{T}\leq\frac{1}{2}. $$

The Sauer–Shelah lemma says that if $\mathcal{F}$ shatters no set of size $s$ , then

$$ |\mathcal{F}|\leq\sum_{i=0}^{s-1}\binom{M}{i}\leq\exp\bigl(MH_{2}(s/M)\bigr)\leq\exp\bigl(TfH_{2}(4/T)\bigr)\text{.} $$

The entropy slack $\gamma>TH_{2}(4/T)$ in Theorem A.35 makes this strictly smaller than $e^{\gamma f}\leq|\mathcal{F}|$ . Hence $\mathcal{F}$ shatters a coordinate set $S$ of size at least $(3C_{\rm ar}+2)b$ .

Each rational-prime label contributes exactly $f\leq 3C_{\rm ar}b$ coordinates. Our goal is to find a subset of $S$ of size at least $2b$ that contains at most $b$ coordinates of each rational-prime label. If at least two labels have more than $b$ selected coordinates in $S$ , then after truncation those two labels alone contribute $2b$ retained coordinates. If at most one label has more than $b$ selected coordinates in $S$ , then the total number lost is at most $f-b\leq(3C_{\rm ar}-1)b$ , so the retained number is at least

$$ (3C_{\rm ar}+2)b-(3C_{\rm ar}-1)b=3b. $$

Thus in all cases at least $2b$ coordinates remain, and no label occurs more than $b$ times among them. Retain exactly $2b$ of the surviving coordinates. This retained set is a subset of the shattered set $S$ , and hence is itself shattered.

We claim that these coordinates can be partitioned into $b$ pairs whose two members have distinct rational-prime labels. Indeed, suppose an even number $2m$ of coordinates remain and every label class has size at most $m$ . If the maximum multiplicity is exactly $m$ , then at most two label classes have this multiplicity. Remove one coordinate from a largest label class and one coordinate from a different largest class if there are two, or from any different label class if there is only one; in the one-largest-class case such a different class exists whenever $m>0$ , because only $m$ of the $2m$ coordinates have the largest label. All remaining label classes then have size at most $m-1$ . If the maximum multiplicity is already less than $m$ , then it is at most $m-1$ ; remove any two coordinates with distinct labels, which exist unless $m=0$ . Again every remaining label class has size at most $m-1$ , half of the remaining $2m-2$ coordinates. Induction on $m$ (beginning with $m=b$ ) proves the claim.

Label the resulting pairs by $j=1,\ldots,b$ , and write the two coordinates in the $j$ th pair as $m(j,1)$ and $m(j,2)$ . For each $r\in\{1,2\}$ , define the selected prime ideal

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{j,r}:=\begin{cases}\mathfrak{P}_{m(j,r)}&\text{if }\eta_{m(j,r)}=0,\\
c\mathfrak{P}_{m(j,r)}&\text{if }\eta_{m(j,r)}=1.\end{cases} $$

Now fix $a\in\{0,1\}^{b}$ . For each selected coordinate $m(j,r)$ prescribe the bit

$$ \theta_{j,r}(a):=\begin{cases}a_{j}&\text{if }\eta_{m(j,r)}=0,\\
1-a_{j}&\text{if }\eta_{m(j,r)}=1.\end{cases} $$

Because the retained coordinates form a shattered subset of $S$ , there exists $\varepsilon(a)\in\mathcal{F}$ with

$$ \varepsilon(a)_{m(j,r)}=\theta_{j,r}(a)\qquad\text{for all }j\in[b],\ r\in\{1,2\}. $$

Define $u_{a}:=u_{\varepsilon(a)}$ . If $\eta_{m(j,r)}=0$ , then

$$ \operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(u_{a})=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}_{m(j,r)}}(u_{\varepsilon(a)})=2(\varepsilon(a)_{m(j,r)}-\eta_{m(j,r)})=2a_{j}. $$

If $\eta_{m(j,r)}=1$ , then

$$ \operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(u_{a})=\operatorname{val}_{c\mathfrak{P}_{m(j,r)}}(u_{\varepsilon(a)})=-2(\varepsilon(a)_{m(j,r)}-\eta_{m(j,r)})=2a_{j}. $$

In both cases the conjugate prime has valuation $-2a_{j}$ , so (2)–(3) hold. The two rational-prime labels assigned to bit $j$ are distinct and both lie in $[Y,2Y]$ , so their product is at least $Y^{2}>L$ . Finally, $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=2f\leq 6C_{\rm ar}b$ , so the degree bound follows after setting $C_{0}:=6C_{\rm ar}$ . ∎

## Appendix B Reductions from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV

In this appendix, we give reductions from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV to $\mathbb{Z}$ -Max-IP, Furthest Pair, and Bichromatic Closest Pair for completeness.

#### Lemma B.1 (Implicit in [Wil18], Theorem 4.3 in [Che20]).

There is an $O(n\operatorname{poly}(r))$ -time reduction from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV in dimension $r$ to exact $\mathbb{Z}$ -Max-IP in dimension $O(r^{2})$ . If the $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV coordinates have bit-length $B$ , then the produced $\mathbb{Z}$ -Max-IP coordinates have bit-length $O(B)$ .

#### Proof.

Represent

$$ P(x,y)=-(x\cdot y)^{2}=-\sum_{i,j}x_{i}x_{j}y_{i}y_{j} $$

as an ordinary inner product in dimension $r^{2}$ , for example by mapping $x$ to coordinates $x_{i}x_{j}$ and $y$ to coordinates $-y_{i}y_{j}$ . Then $P(x,y)\leq 0$ for all pairs, and $P(x,y)=0$ exactly when $x\cdot y=0$ . Thus a zero inner product exists in the $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV instance iff the maximum produced inner product is $0$ . Products of two $B$ -bit integers have $O(B)$ bits, so the bit-length stays $O(B)$ . ∎

Next, we give a reduction from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV to Furthest Pair, which is based on [Wil18, Theorem 1.2].

#### Lemma B.2.

There is an $O(n\operatorname{poly}(r))$ -time reduction from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV in dimension $r$ to Furthest Pair in dimension $O(r^{2})$ . If the $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV coordinates have bit-length $B$ , then the produced Furthest Pair coordinates have bit-length $O(B+\log r)$ .

#### Proof.

We first run the reduction in Lemma B.1 to obtain a $\mathbb{Z}$ -Max-IP instance in dimension $O(r^{2})$ between sets of vectors $U$ and $V$ , where $u\cdot v\leq 0$ for $u\in U$ and $v\in V$ , and the goal is to determine if the maximum dot product is $0$ . If there is any zero vector, the maximum dot product is trivially $0$ . So in the following, we assume all vectors are nonzero.

Let $C$ be a sufficiently large integer. For any $u\in U$ and $v\in V$ , define

$$ u^{\prime}=(u/\lVert u\rVert_{2},C,0),v^{\prime}=(-v/\lVert v\rVert_{2},0,C). $$

Let the set of $u^{\prime}$ and $v^{\prime}$ be the Furthest Pair instance.

For $u_{1}^{\prime}$ and $u_{2}^{\prime}$ , their squared distance is

$$ \lVert u_{1}^{\prime}-u_{2}^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}=\lVert u_{1}/\lVert u_{1}\rVert_{2}-u_{2}/\lVert u_{2}\rVert_{2}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 4, $$

and similarly,

$$ \lVert v_{1}^{\prime}-v_{2}^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 4. $$

Next consider

$$ \lVert u^{\prime}-v^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}=\lVert u^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lVert v^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}-2u^{\prime}\cdot v^{\prime}=2(C^{2}+1)+\frac{2u\cdot v}{\lVert u\rVert_{2}\lVert v\rVert_{2}}. $$

For large enough $C$ , the furthest pair must be $u^{\prime},v^{\prime}$ for some $u\in U$ and $v\in V$ . Furthermore, if the furthest pair has squared distance $2(C^{2}+1)$ , then there exists $u\in U,v\in V$ with $u\cdot v=0$ ; otherwise, there does not exist such pair.

The above completes the reduction to Furthest Pair with real coordinates. To convert the vectors to integer coordinates, first consider if $u\cdot v<0$ , then

$$ \frac{u\cdot v}{\lVert u\rVert_{2}\lVert v\rVert_{2}}\leq-\frac{1}{\operatorname{poly}(r)\cdot 2^{O(B)}}. $$

Let $\Delta$ be the absolute value of the above gap. Next, choose $\delta>0$ be some small real number to be determined. If we round each coordinate $z$ to a nearest multiple $k(z)\delta$ of $\delta$ for $k(z)\in\mathbb{Z}$ , then the squared distance between any two vectors can change by at most $O(\delta r^{2})$ . Hence, we can have $\delta=O(\Delta/r^{2})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{poly}(r)\cdot 2^{O(B)}}$ , so that the squared distance between any two vectors changes by at most $\Delta/2$ . This way, we can determine whether the maximum inner product before rounding is $0$ , by checking whether the maximum inner product after rounding is larger than $-\Delta/2$ . Finally, after rounding $z$ to $k(z)\delta$ , output the integer coordinate $k(z)$ to obtain integer vectors. ∎

Finally, we give a reduction from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV to Bichromatic Closest Pair, which is based on [Wil18, Corollary 2.1].

#### Lemma B.3.

There is an $O(n\operatorname{poly}(r))$ -time reduction from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV in dimension $r$ to Bichromatic Closest Pair in dimension $O(r^{2})$ . If the $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV coordinates have bit-length $B$ , then the produced Bichromatic Closest Pair coordinates have bit-length $O(B+\log r)$ .

#### Proof.

We first run the reduction in Lemma B.1 to obtain a $\mathbb{Z}$ -Max-IP instance in dimension $O(r^{2})$ between sets of vectors $U$ and $V$ , where $u\cdot v\leq 0$ for $u\in U$ and $v\in V$ , and the goal is to determine if the maximum dot product is $0$ . If there is any zero vector, the maximum dot product is trivially $0$ . So in the following, we assume all vectors are nonzero.

For any $u\in U$ and $v\in V$ , define

$$ u^{\prime}=u/\lVert u\rVert_{2},v^{\prime}=v/\lVert v\rVert_{2}. $$

Let $U^{\prime}=\{u^{\prime}:u\in U\}$ and $V^{\prime}=\{v^{\prime}:v\in V\}$ be the input to Bichromatic Closest Pair.

Consider

$$ \lVert u^{\prime}-v^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}=\lVert u^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lVert v^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}-2u^{\prime}\cdot v^{\prime}=2-\frac{2u\cdot v}{\lVert u\rVert_{2}\lVert v\rVert_{2}}. $$

If the closest pair has squared distance $2$ , then there exists $u\in U,v\in V$ with $u\cdot v=0$ ; otherwise, there does not exist such pair.

The above completes the reduction to Bichromatic Closest Pair with real coordinates. The vectors can be rounded to integers in the same way as Lemma B.2. ∎
